activities.caption: fill the blanks — expand the acronym
activities.name: dsgeAcronymCloze

config.text: DSGE stands for %%0%% (agents choose over time with expectations), %%1%% (random shocks push them around) and general equilibrium (all markets clear at once). Built from optimising agents, it is the language modern macro uses for %%2%% analysis.
config.hint: Time, randomness and simultaneous markets — each word buys something.

activities.anchor: the four steps are the model's construction sequence
activities.caption: build the DSGE machine, in order
activities.name: dsgeBuildOrder

config.prompt: Put the DSGE construction sequence in order:
items: Add sticky prices so money has short-run power
Fit the whole machine to data
Hand it to central banks for policy counterfactuals
config.why: Each section of the lesson lives inside one of these four steps; the sequence is construction, not a menu.

activities.anchor: model the agents, not the aggregates
activities.caption: pair each Lucas-critique idea with its claim
activities.name: dsgeLucasMatch

config.prompt: Pair each Lucas-critique idea with its claim:

pairs.right: estimated relationships break when policy changes the decision rules
model the agents, not the aggregates, so policy enters as a rule
a government optimising afresh each period promises one thing and does another
a credible rule can beat fresh optimisation, even for a well-intentioned policymaker

config.why: The critique forced macro to build from optimising agents; time inconsistency is its policy corollary.

activities.anchor: the Lucas critique means every estimated
activities.caption: find the overreach
activities.name: dsgeLucasSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the Lucas-critique reasoning goes too far:
lines: The Lucas critique says estimated relationships reflect behaviour under the old policy regime.
Therefore every estimated relationship is useless for any purpose.
It bites specifically when a policy change alters the decision rules generating the data.
For short-horizon forecasting within an unchanged regime, estimated relationships remain useful.
The critique disciplines structural claims, not all empirics.
config.correction: The critique bites when policy changes the decision rules, not on every estimate.
config.why: It disciplines structural claims; short-horizon forecasting within a regime still works.

activities.anchor: That is why simulated multipliers are state-dependent
activities.caption: one stimulus, two monetary states
activities.name: dsgeMultiplierCompare

config.prompt: One stimulus, two monetary states — drag the divider:

before.label: normal monetary response
before.text: a 1% of GDP spending boost raises output by roughly 0.9–1.5%

after.label: zero lower bound
after.text: with rates pinned and no offsetting tightening, the same stimulus does several times more work

config.why: The multiplier is a property of the whole system — monetary reaction, borrowing constraints, tax distortions — not a number a government can assume.

activities.anchor: with inflation at 4% and output 1% above trend
activities.caption: mark the prescribed policy rate
activities.name: dsgeTaylorPlace

config.prompt: Using the Taylor rule, with inflation at 4%, a 2% target and output 1% above trend, what policy rate is prescribed? Place it.
config.why: 2 + 4 + 0.5×(4−2) + 0.5×1 = 7.5%. The rule is the benchmark; deviations are explainable judgement.

activities.anchor: In the model, supply-side conditions appear as two kinds of object
activities.caption: shock, parameter or state?
activities.name: dsgeObjectSort

config.prompt: Which object is each item in the model?
config.why: Shocks drive the cycle, parameters govern steady-state behaviour, and states are what the model solves for.

activities.anchor: studies of individual price records find many
activities.caption: call the average price duration
activities.name: dsgeDurationEst

config.prompt: Micro-evidence finds many prices changing only every 6–12 months. What is the midpoint of that range, in months?
config.why: 9 months is the midpoint. Calvo pricing with θ = 0.75 implies an average duration of 1/(1−0.75) = 4 quarters, squarely in the empirical range.
config.context: sticky prices are why a nominal rate move moves the real rate

config.root: The standard search-and-matching model generates only about a tenth of the observed volatility in unemployment. Trace the repair.

choices.label: Wage rigidity and outside options that make hiring respond more strongly
choices.feedback: Yes — the standard wage bargain absorbs too much of the shock.

choices.label: Nothing — the data must be wrong
choices.feedback: The volatility is measured robustly; the model is the problem.

choices.label: More shocks, of any kind
choices.feedback: Adding shocks without changing the labour-market structure does not fix the puzzle.

wage.text: Wage rigidity and outside options are the standard repairs; HANK goes further, giving households different wealth and liquid-asset positions.

data.text: The puzzle is a robust feature of the data, not a measurement error.

shocks.text: The issue is the transmission mechanism, not the number of shocks.

config.why: The labour market is far more cyclical than the benchmark allows; fixing the wage bargain — or modelling heterogeneity — remains live work.

activities.caption: true or false — what the models missed
activities.name: dsgeCrisisJudge

statements.s: The standard DSGE models before 2008 had no meaningful banking sector, household debt or house prices.
statements.why: The crisis hit precisely where the models were blind.

statements.s: The 2008 crisis hit precisely where the models were blind.
statements.why: Queen Elizabeth's question at the LSE made the point publicly.

statements.s: Post-2008 work has produced one consensus model that all central banks now use.
statements.why: Financial-friction DSGE, HANK and hybrid systems coexist; there is no single consensus model.

statements.s: Central banks run DSGE/VAR ensembles because no single model earns full trust.
statements.why: The ensemble is the field's mature answer to model uncertainty.
